question: A back-office team plans to remove three handoffs between reviewers by having Claude carry each case straight through. Those handoffs are also where colleagues currently catch one another's mistakes. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) Reviewers may resist a change that removes part of what they currently do each day.
B) The informal checks that lived in those handoffs disappear with nothing put in their place.
C) The redesigned process may be considerably harder to explain to auditors than the version it replaces.
D) The time saved may be less than expected once the new process is running at full volume.
correct_answers: B) The informal checks that lived in those handoffs disappear with nothing put in their place.
explanations: Resistance to change is common and is addressed by involving the reviewers in the redesign. It affects how smoothly the change lands rather than whether the resulting process is safe.

Correct. The handoffs were doing two jobs, and only the visible one is being replaced. Removing them takes out the peer review that was catching errors, so the redesigned process is not just faster but materially less accurate unless a deliberate check is designed back in.
Explaining a new process to auditors takes documentation effort and is a normal part of any change. It becomes a serious problem only because of the missing checks, which is the underlying issue.
A smaller saving than hoped would make the change less worthwhile, which is disappointing but recoverable. The team would still be able to see the shortfall and adjust.
